title: SYSK Selects: Will Computers Replace Doctors?
summary: SYSK Selects episode, introduced by Josh, rerunning the 'Will Computers Replace Doctors?' discussion. Hosts explore whether computers and AI could take over parts of medicine: consumer health tracking wearables, the 2011 World Science Festival avatar kiosk that handled a baby's diarrhea case, the claim that computers may have better consistent bedside manner, IBM's Watson and its natural-language strengths for diagnosis, Dr. Dolly Wall and the Isabel diagnostic program (inspired by his daughter's missed necrotizing fasciitis), diagnostic error statistics, robotic surgery with da Vinci and the FDA's underreporting of injuries (including the Sheina Wilson case), and emerging self-diagnostic smartphone tools. They conclude humans will still be needed but robots will assist. The episode closes with listener mail about white clover, dandelions and the Scott Fertilizer Company redefining weeds, followed by the sign-off.

segments.title: Selects intro and welcome
segments.summary: Josh introduces this week's SYSK Selects pick, 'Will Computers Replace Doctors?', noting it was recorded years ago. Chuck and Josh chat about the cold weather and the holidays.

segments.title: Consumer health tracking and informed patients
segments.summary: The hosts discuss wearables such as Fitbit, Nike FuelBand and Jawbone, apps that track mood and sleep, and the growing desire of people to monitor their own health and use data to decide when to see a doctor.

segments.title: Future of physicians and expert opinions
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck survey opinions on whether physicians will be replaced. Kent Bottles thinks GPs could be replaced by diagnostic computers, possibly with avatars. Farhad Manjoo argues specialists are more vulnerable than GPs. A columnist suggests nurses could be the human interface between robots and patients.

segments.title: Avatars and bedside manner
segments.summary: A 2011 World Science Festival kiosk avatar handled a mother's query about a baby's diarrhea, deciding it was not urgent and booking a later appointment; the mother preferred it to hospital nurses. The hosts discuss consistency of programmed empathy and a study where anxiety patients disclosed more to an avatar than to a psychiatrist.

segments.title: Personal care and medical history
segments.summary: The hosts compare modern impersonal care with the family doctor who knew a patient's history. They note that intimate knowledge of medical history is largely lost in modern practice, a area where computers could potentially do better.

segments.title: Watson, diagnostic software and natural language
segments.summary: Diagnostic software dates to the 1970s at the University of Pittsburgh, and MASS General's DXplain provides ranked diagnoses. IBM's Watson, which won at Jeopardy, is discussed for treatment options and its handling of natural language in medical records, along with the ability to process vast literature quickly while doctors have limited reading time.

segments.title: Dr. Dolly Wall, Isabel and misdiagnosis
segments.summary: Dr. Dolly Wall is described as a diagnostic savant who performs on stage. He uses the Isabel program, which he says has never offered a diagnosis he missed. Physician habits and forgotten training are discussed, along with the claim that one in five US diagnoses is incorrect or incomplete, and the role of intuition versus data.

segments.title: Isabel origin and diagnostic assistants
segments.summary: The Isabel program was named after the creator's daughter, who was misdiagnosed with chicken pox when she actually had necrotizing fasciitis. A company called Life Calm reported clinical trials where diagnostic engines were accurate using symptoms alone. The hosts agree such tools make sense as assistants to physicians.

segments.title: Robotic surgery and FDA injury reporting
segments.summary: Robotic surgery has been performed since the early 1980s, and the da Vinci system is described, with a surgeon controlling robotic arms. The first fully robotic prostate removal occurred in Montreal in 2010. Concerns include underreporting of injuries to the FDA, the Sheina Wilson hysterectomy case, and the need for adequate surgeon training.

segments.title: Self-diagnosis tools and personalized medicine
segments.summary: The hosts discuss smartphone-based tools such as a portable ECG, attachments for skin and ear imaging, an eye test device, and a breath sensor for cancer detection, plus dogs or bees trained to detect cancer. They discuss proteonomics and genomics as a path to personalized treatment, and conclude that humans will still be needed but robots will assist.

segments.title: Listener mail: Weeds and white clover
segments.summary: Listener Robert Paulson writes that white clover and dandelions were once standard lawn plants, and that Scott Fertilizer Company redefined them as weeds after its products killed them.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh invites listeners to get in touch and promotes the show's website and social channels.
